# Two-stage classification of avalanche problems and danger levels across elevation bands in Colorado

- J S

Justin Schwartzreich 1 * 
- I F

Ivan Felipe Rodriguez 2 

- 1. School of Computer Science, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, United States
- 2. Cognitive Sciences Department, Brown University, Providence, RI, United States

## Abstract

Avalanches threaten the lives of winter backcountry travelers across the globe, yet many high-risk zones lack the instrumentation infrastructure required by feature-rich avalanche forecasting frameworks. We propose a two-stage machine learning classification framework that first predicts the presence of three distinct avalanche problem types (Slab Problem, Persistent Slab, and Loose Wet) and then uses these intermediate predictions, together with meteorological and derived snowpack features, to estimate the overall avalanche danger level. The framework is trained and evaluated on a dataset of 28,140 region-band-days spanning eight Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecast regions and the 2013–2022 winter seasons, using meteorological inputs derived exclusively from publicly available NOAA Global Historical Climatology Network–Daily stations. Architectures are trained separately for each of three elevation bands (below treeline, near treeline, and above treeline), with forecast region included as a one-hot feature to preserve site-level structure within a pooled training dataset, and models are evaluated using a staged chronological splitting protocol with separate held-out windows for Stage-1 and Stage-2 model selection. The framework outperforms a Pérez-Guillén-style Random Forest reproduction on the same eight-zone Colorado dataset by +0.131 macro-F1 averaged across elevation bands, with non-overlapping bootstrap 95% confidence intervals at every band. On the subset of days when the issued danger rating changes from the previous day, when forecasters are actively reassessing conditions, the framework significantly outperforms both climatology and 1-day persistence at every elevation band (paired permutation p < 0.001). The most operationally consequential result concerns High-danger (Class 3) prediction, where the framework achieves Class 3 F1 of 0.341, 0.457, and 0.504 across the three elevation bands, compared with 0.094 for a best-tuned Random Forest baseline on the same data. These results demonstrate that operationally meaningful avalanche hazard signal can be extracted from widely available meteorological observations when paired with operationally informed architectural design, expanding the potential for data-driven avalanche forecasting in regions that lack specialized atmospheric or snowpack instrumentation.

## 1 Introduction

As shown in Winkler et al. (2016), avalanches remain one of the leading causes of fatalities during winter backcountry recreation. In the United States last year, 22 people were killed in avalanche accidents, and 107 individuals were caught in avalanches in Colorado alone. Globally, additional fatalities occur each season, though reporting is inconsistent across countries. Most avalanches originate from either the collapse of a weak layer beneath a cohesive slab or wet‐snow processes in which meltwater weakens stratigraphy within an isothermal snowpack. A third type, loose avalanches, occurs when unconsolidated surface snow slides, gaining mass as it descends the slope.

To the winter backcountry traveler, knowing what types of problems to look for and the general risk of a given day are integral parts of decision making and safety. In select developed, snowy, mountainous regions, there are avalanche forecasting centers who conduct field observations to assess the danger and existing problems for a given day, as shown by Degawa and Hirota (2008) and Winkler et al. (2021). From 2014–2024 Logan et al. (2024), showed that 42 out of 197 fatal avalanches (killing 225 people) occurred in backcountry zones where there was no forecast. Without the forecast, backcountry travelers lose information on daily hazards, which can be critical to their decisions and safety.

Machine learning and deep learning approaches offer a promising pathway for expanding avalanche forecasting accessibility by enabling predictions derived from widely available meteorological observations. Several studies have explored statistical and machine-learning methods for avalanche prediction. Early work by Schirmer et al. (2009) demonstrated regional danger forecasting using simulated snow-cover data, while more recent studies have applied machine-learning models to predict avalanche danger levels and activity using meteorological and snowpack predictors (e.g., Pérez-Guillén et al., 2022; Dkengne Sielenou et al. (2021), Mayer et al. (2023)). Other research has investigated snow instability characterization through avalanche problem types derived from physical simulations (Reuter et al., 2022) and regional statistical modeling frameworks (Eiselt and Graversen, 2025). These approaches demonstrate the growing potential of data-driven avalanche forecasting but typically rely on extensive feature sets, snowpack simulations, or single-stage prediction frameworks.

Operational avalanche forecasts, however, are inherently structured around avalanche problems, which describe the dominant failure mechanisms, followed by an integrated danger rating reflecting likelihood and consequence (Statham et al., 2018). Existing machine-learning studies generally predict danger levels directly, without explicitly modeling the intermediate problem structure used by forecasters. Furthermore, many approaches depend on specialized atmospheric or snowpack variables such as wind transport, radiation, or detailed stratigraphy that are unavailable in data-sparse regions.

In this study, we propose a two-stage classification framework that first predicts the presence of key avalanche problem types and subsequently predicts overall avalanche danger using those predictions as structured inputs. This design more closely mirrors operational forecasting workflows while enabling prediction using reduced meteorology-only feature sets. We evaluate this framework across multiple altitude bands in Colorado’s continental snow climate, allowing investigation of elevation-dependent hazard dynamics.

Our contributions are fourfold. First, we introduce a two-stage machine-learning architecture that explicitly models avalanche problems prior to danger-level prediction. Second, we evaluate model performance across multiple elevation bands, capturing altitude-dependent differences in avalanche formation processes. Third, we demonstrate that competitive predictive performance can be achieved using widely available meteorological variables—including temperature, snowfall aggregates, and simplified snowpack estimates—without reliance on specialized atmospheric inputs. Finally, this work provides a systematic evaluation of data-driven avalanche prediction within a continental snow climate, offering insight into scalable forecasting approaches for regions lacking operational avalanche services.

## 2 Methods

In this paper, we develop and evaluate a two-stage machine-learning framework for predicting avalanche hazard across eight CAIC forecast regions in Colorado. We pair raw daily meteorological observations from co-located NOAA stations with operational forecast labels and adjust observed snowfall and temperature to each of three elevation bands, below treeline (BTL), near treeline (NTL), and above treeline (ATL), using physically motivated relationships. Stage 1 predicts the presence of three distinct avalanche problem types, Slab Problem (the union of storm slab and wind slab), Persistent Slab, and Loose Wet, that together capture the dominant dry-snow and melt-driven failure mechanisms in the dataset. Stage 2 uses these problem-type predictions, together with the meteorological and snowpack features, to estimate the overall avalanche danger rating. Models are trained and evaluated using a staged chronological splitting protocol with separate held-out windows for each stage, as detailed in §2.1.4.

### 2.1 Dataset

To develop and evaluate the proposed framework, we constructed a combined meteorological and avalanche-forecast dataset derived entirely from publicly available observational sources in Colorado, United States. Meteorological data were obtained from the NOAA Global Historical Climatology Network–Daily (GHCN-Daily) archive using raw TMAX, TMIN, and snowfall records without intermediate smoothing or filtering. Avalanche danger ratings and problem classifications were obtained from the Colorado Avalanche Information Center (CAIC) daily forecast archive.

The dataset spans the winter seasons from 2013 through 2022, covering eight representative forecast regions within Colorado’s continental snow climate: Steamboat & Flat Tops, Front Range, Vail & Summit County, Sawatch Range, Aspen, Grand Mesa, Gunnison, and Northern San Juan. These regions were selected because they represent well-instrumented mountainous environments with consistent operational avalanche forecasts and diverse elevation-dependent snowpack behavior; however, Grand Mesa is a lower-altitude region, so the forecast only covers Below Treeline and Near Treeline. #### 2.1.1 Elevation bands

CAIC forecasts report avalanche danger across elevation zones rather than single altitudes. To align meteorological observations with operational forecasting practice, three elevation bands were defined:

- Below Treeline (BTL): approximately 10,500 ft
- Near Treeline (NTL): approximately 11,500 ft
- Above Treeline (ATL): approximately 12,500 ft

These elevation bands are derived from the central points of Colorado’s tree coverage in mountainous regions. Because NOAA stations are located between approximately 8,000–9,000 ft, meteorological variables were adjusted to each elevation band using physically motivated snowfall scaling and temperature lapse-rate corrections (Sections 2.2–2.3). Figure 2 is a visualization of these different elevation bands with respect to treeline.

FIGURE 2

A visualization of how altitude, temperature, and weather features affect the Colorado snowpack to form the given avalanche problems, additionally highlighting the formation of each problem and an explanation of overall danger. Credit to the Colorado Avalanche Information Center for the avalanche problem diagrams.

Each of the eight CAIC forecast regions was paired with a single GHCN-Daily station located within or adjacent to the region. Stations were selected to satisfy three criteria: (i) elevation within approximately 1,000–3,000 ft of the lowest target elevation band in the corresponding forecast region, (ii) continuous daily reporting of TMAX, TMIN, and snowfall across the study period, and (iii) preference for stations on the windward side of the relevant range to avoid lee-side precipitation shadowing.

#### 2.1.2 Data aggregation and samples

Daily observations were used rather than hourly records to reduce noise and missing values associated with high-frequency SNOTEL measurements (Avanzi et al., 2014). Each record in the dataset represents a single day at a specific region and elevation band, paired with the corresponding CAIC danger rating. The final dataset contains daily meteorological features, derived snowpack variables, binary avalanche problem labels (Persistent Slab, Slab Problem, and Loose Wet), and multiclass avalanche danger ratings. All regions were pooled into a unified dataset to increase statistical robustness while preserving elevation-dependent variability through altitude-adjusted features.

#### 2.1.3 Target variables

Two prediction targets were defined: Stage 1 (Avalanche Problems) and Stage 2 (Overall Avalanche Danger). Avalanche danger ratings were derived from the North American Public Avalanche Danger Scale (1–5). For machine-learning compatibility, labels were remapped to a zero-indexed classification scheme by subtracting one from each issued danger level, resulting in four operational classes ranging from 0 (Low) to 3 (High). Class 4 (Extreme) and days without an issued operational rating were excluded; Class 4 did not occur in the dataset over the study period.

#### 2.1.4 Dataset splitting

To prevent temporal leakage, we implemented a 40/10/45/7.5/7.5 split across two stages. Stage 1 was trained on data in the range 0%–40% and evaluated on the range 40%–50%, where the best model in this range is selected for each Stage 1 problem. To avoid training on overfit predictions from Stage 1, we then trained the Stage 2 models from 40% to 85%, using the frozen snapshots from the Stage 1 models. The Stage 2 models were then evaluated on two separate holdout periods: 85%–92.5% and 92.5%–100%.

The Stage-1 evaluation window (40%–50%) and the Stage-2 training window (40%–85%) share a 10% overlap, but this overlap does not introduce leakage into Stage-2 training: the Stage-1 models that generate features for Stage 2 were never trained on any portion of the 40%–85% range, so their predictions on the 40%–50% subrange are out-of-sample with respect to Stage 1 even when that subrange is used to train Stage 2.

Headline performance results in §3 are reported as the mean of both Stage-2 out of sample windows. Reporting the mean of two adjacent held-out windows preserves comparability with single-split evaluation paradigms such as Pérez-Guillén et al. (2022) while also providing visibility into validation-versus-test stability, which we discuss as a limitation in §4.6.

The predictor variables were designed to capture the primary physical mechanisms governing avalanche formation and can be interpreted through three complementary categories. First, short-term loading indicators, including daily snowfall as well as three- and 7-day cumulative snowfall totals, represent rapid storm-driven loading events that contribute to slab formation. Second, snowpack state variables, such as modeled snowpack depth and rolling snowpack accumulation metrics, describe the evolving seasonal structure of the snowpack and provide context for longer-term stability conditions. Third, temperature-derived predictors, including rolling maximum and minimum temperatures and multi-day temperature means, capture melt–freeze cycles and sustained cold periods that influence weak-layer development and persistence. Together, these variables provide a simplified yet physically interpretable representation of avalanche formation processes derived solely from widely available meteorological observations.

The dataset exhibits the class imbalance characteristic of operational avalanche forecasting records. After preprocessing and label remapping, Low danger conditions comprise 30.55% of observations, Moderate danger accounts for 50.01%, and Considerable danger represents 17.17% of the dataset. Higher hazard conditions are comparatively rare, with High danger occurring in 2.27% of observations. Consequently, Moderate and Considerable danger levels together account for approximately 67.18% of all samples, while the most hazardous conditions remain infrequent. This imbalance reflects the natural climatological distribution of avalanche danger rather than sampling bias and is consistent with continental snow climates, where extreme instability develops only during limited periods of intense loading or persistent weak-layer activation.

### 2.2 Altitude-adjusted snowfall

Because NOAA station elevations in our dataset were generally between 8,000 and 9,000 ft, while the target CAIC elevation bands were approximately 10,500, 11,500, and 12,500 ft, altitude-based adjustment was required to align station observations with forecast elevation zones. To estimate snowfall at each target elevation band, we applied an orographic scaling relationship derived from (Judson and Doesken, 2000): where M is the orographic snowfall multiplier, Elev base, is the elevation of the NOAA station (ft), Elev band, is the representative elevation of the target CAIC band (ft), Snow base,t is the observed daily snowfall at the station for a given day, t, and Snow band,t is the altitude-adjusted daily snowfall for the target elevation band. Equations 1, 2 are used in ensemble to first find the orographic multiplier and then apply it to the base snowfall to derive the altitude-adjusted snowfall.

### 2.3 Altitude-adjusted temperature

To account for the decrease in temperature with elevation, we adjusted station temperatures using a lapse rate of 6.1 °C km -1, based on Barry (2008). The 6.1 °C km -1 value used here is the environmental (free-air) lapse rate reported by Barry (2008) for mid-latitude mountain environments, not the dry adiabatic (≈9.8 °C km -1) or pseudo-adiabatic (≈5 °C km -1) rates. It represents the climatological mean lapse rate observed in the Colorado Rockies and is intended as a single first-order adjustment between station and band elevations; variable lapse rates are discussed as a limitation in §4.6. ### 2.5 Classification method

To predict avalanche hazard conditions, we implemented a two-stage supervised classification framework designed to reflect the structure of operational avalanche forecasting. Rather than predicting overall avalanche danger directly, the framework first identifies dominant avalanche problems and subsequently predicts the integrated danger rating using these intermediate outputs as structured inputs.

#### 2.5.1 Two-stage framework

Operational avalanche forecasts describe hazard through two related components: (i) the presence of avalanche problems representing dominant failure mechanisms, and (ii) an overall danger rating summarizing likelihood and consequence. To approximate this workflow, classification is performed sequentially. Stage 1 produces binary predictions for each of three avalanche problem types—Slab Problem, Persistent Slab, and Loose Wet—at each elevation band. Stage 2 then uses these problem predictions, together with the meteorological and derived snowpack features, to predict the four-class overall danger rating at the same elevation band.

#### 2.5.2 Stage 1 classification

Binary classifiers were trained to predict the presence or absence of the three most prevalent avalanche problem categories in the study dataset: Persistent Slab, Slab Problem, and Loose Wet. The Slab Problem target merged storm slab and wind slab into a single binary class because the available meteorological dataset did not include wind speed or wind direction, preventing reliable separation of wind-transport-driven slab formation from storm-loading-driven slab formation. Accordingly, this class should be interpreted as a generalized slab-instability indicator rather than a physically explicit wind slab classifier. While both storm slab and wind slab involve cohesive slab release associated with recent loading, the absence of wind predictors limits mechanistic specificity and may reduce performance on days when wind transport is the dominant driver.

Separate models were trained for each elevation band (BTL, NTL, and ATL) because avalanche formation processes vary substantially with altitude due to temperature gradients, snowfall distribution, and treeline effects. This resulted in nine Stage-1 models: three problem types across three elevation bands.

#### 2.5.3 Stage 2 classification

Predictions from Stage 1 were incorporated as additional input features alongside meteorological and derived snowpack variables to predict the overall avalanche danger rating. This design allows the second-stage model to condition danger estimates on inferred physical processes rather than raw weather variables alone. The approach serves as a structured approximation of forecasting practice rather than a causal representation, as operational danger ratings also depend on expert judgment, avalanche size, and spatial variability.

Critically, Stage 2 never receives the forecaster-issued problem labels. The problem-type features consumed at Stage 2 are predictions from the frozen Stage-1 ensembles described in §2.5.5, which are functions of the meteorological and snowpack inputs alone and are generated out-of-sample with respect to Stage-1 training. The danger model therefore conditions on inferred failure mechanisms derived from weather, not on any label co-issued with the danger rating it is trained to predict.

In total, twelve classification models were trained: three Persistent Slab models, three Slab Problem models, three Loose Wet models, and three Overall Danger models corresponding to the three elevation bands. See Figure 3 for a visualization of the modeling pipeline.

#### 2.5.4 Model families

Because it was not clear in advance which modeling approach would perform best for avalanche prediction, both tree-based ensemble models and deep learning models were tested. Tree-based methods were included because they handle nonlinear relationships well and perform reliably with meteorological data that contain correlated variables and mixed feature scales. The ensemble models evaluated in this study included ExtraTrees, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM. These models were used to learn relationships between snowfall, temperature trends, and snowpack conditions without requiring extensive preprocessing or feature normalization.

In addition to ensemble methods, several neural network architectures were evaluated to determine whether explicitly modeling temporal patterns improves prediction performance. Avalanche conditions develop over multiple days, so recurrent neural networks were trained to capture time-dependent relationships in the data. The architectures tested included Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM), Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), and Simple Recurrent Neural Networks (SimpleRNN). Transformer models were also evaluated to test whether attention-based approaches could better capture longer-term dependencies in meteorological conditions.

These model families allowed comparison between traditional machine-learning approaches and sequence-based deep learning models within the same prediction framework.

#### 2.5.5 Training procedure

All models were trained using the staged chronological splitting protocol described in §2.1.4, in which the dataset is divided into five contiguous windows: Stage-1 training (0%–40%), Stage-1 evaluation (40%–50%), Stage-2 training (40%–85%), Stage-2 validation (85%–92.5%), and Stage-2 test (92.5%–100%). To prevent temporal leakage, oversampling for class imbalance was applied only within training windows using a random oversampler, leaving all held-out evaluation windows at their natural class distributions. This train-only resampling strategy follows established practice for class-imbalanced classification, where rebalancing is confined to training data so that evaluation reflects the true operational class distribution (Blanchard et al., 2022).

For Stage 1, each candidate architecture–hyperparameter configuration was trained on the Stage-1 training window and scored on the Stage-1 evaluation window. For each (band, problem-type) cell, the top three configurations by macro-F1 on the Stage-1 evaluation window were then retained and combined as a soft-voting ensemble, with predictions averaged across the three frozen models. This ensemble was used to generate predicted-problem features for the Stage-2 training, validation, and test windows. Because the Stage-1 models were never trained on any data in the 40%–100% range, their predictions on those windows are out-of-sample with respect to Stage 1, even though the 40%–50% subrange is subsequently used to train Stage 2.

For Stage 2, each candidate configuration was trained on the Stage-2 training window (40%–85%) using meteorological and snowpack features together with the three Stage-1 ensemble predictions, and scored on the Stage-2 validation window for hyperparameter selection. Top-3 soft-voting ensembling was applied at Stage 2 as well, using the validation-window macro-F1 as the selection criterion. Final headline performance is reported as the mean of the Stage-2 validation and test windows, as discussed in §2.1.4.

Tree-based models were trained using standard scikit-learn and XGBoost/LightGBM implementations with grid search over n_estimators ∈ {200, 300, 500, 600} and max_depth ∈ {6, 8, 10, 20, None}. Neural network models were trained using AdamW (learning rate 1 × 10 −3 or 5 × 10 −4, weight decay 1 × 10 −4) with early stopping on the relevant evaluation window (patience = 10 epochs, maximum 100 epochs). Sequence models were trained with a default lookback window of 7 days; longer lookback windows (14 and 30 days) were also evaluated but did not produce a consistent improvement and were not retained in the final configuration sweep, suggesting that the multi-day temporal information already encoded in the rolling-window features substantially overlaps with what explicit sequence modeling can recover.

#### 2.5.6 Model evaluation

Two evaluation procedures are used in this study, and results from each appear in distinct subsections of §3. First, the staged single-split protocol described in §2.1.4 and §2.5.5 is the primary evaluation. This protocol matches the single-split evaluation paradigm used by Pérez-Guillén et al. (2022) and provides separate held-out windows for Stage-1 model selection, Stage-2 model selection, and final test evaluation. Headline Stage-1 and Stage-2 macro-F1 values reported in §3.1 and §3.2 use this protocol, with the mean of the Stage-2 validation and test windows reported as the primary number. All headline macro-F1 values in §3.1, §3.2, and §3.3 are computed by independently evaluating the model on the Stage-2 validation window and the Stage-2 test window and then averaging the two resulting macro-F1 scores. The per-class confusion matrices and metrics reported in the Appendix are instead computed on the val and test windows pooled into a single evaluation set, which yields macro-F1 values that can differ from the headline by approximately 0.01–0.10 because macro-F1 is not invariant under this change of averaging. Headline-table values and appendix per-class metrics are therefore consistent in identifying the best-performing model per cell and in their per-class precision, recall, and support, but their macro-F1 summaries are computed from slightly different aggregations of the same underlying predictions. Second, the models are compared against three reference baselines in §3.3:

Climatology: a per-cell most-frequent-class predictor that always returns the modal label observed in the Stage-2 training window. This represents the floor any non-trivial model must clear.

Persistence: predicts that the current day’s class equals the class issued k days previously, for . Because CAIC ratings are autocorrelated by design (forecasters condition each day’s rating on prior days, and snowpack evolves slowly), persistence at short lags is an unusually strong baseline on full-period evaluation. To distinguish models from autocorrelation, we additionally report performance on the subset of days where the issued rating changes from the previous day (the “transitions-only” evaluation), where 1-day persistence collapses to macro-F1 = 0 by construction. Pérez-Guillén-style Random Forest reproduction: a single Random Forest classifier trained on the pooled three-band dataset using the meteorological and snowpack features together with Forecast Region and elevation-band one-hots, with n_estimators = 500 and max_depth = None, broadly matching the configuration described in Pérez-Guillén et al. (2022). Five additional Random Forest configurations were swept as a sensitivity check. This reproduction is the closest available apples-to-apples comparison between the proposed two-stage per-band framework and a published single-model approach evaluated on the same Colorado dataset.

Statistical significance of model-versus-baseline comparisons is assessed using bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on macro-F1 (10,000 resamples) and paired permutation tests on the per-day macro-F1 differences, with full results reported in §3.3.

## 3 Results

Results are organized into four parts. Across the 9 cells, three architectural patterns emerge that map onto the temporal scale of the underlying physical processes. Tree-based ensembles dominate Slab Problem at every elevation band. #### 3.1.1 Slab problem

Tree-based ensembles achieve the highest macro-F1 for Slab Problem at every elevation band, with XGBoost winning at BTL (0.672) and ATL (0.770), and Random Forest winning at NTL (0.780). This is consistent with the physical drivers of slab instability: storm-slab and wind-slab formation are governed by short-term loading signals—new snow accumulation, recent temperature trends, and bonding conditions in the upper snowpack—that develop over hours to a few days. The 1-, 3-, and 7-day snowfall and temperature aggregates that dominate the feature set are by construction collinear with the underlying daily sequence, which means that sequencing information is already encoded in the tabular representation. The marginal information that explicit sequence modeling can extract over and above the rolling-window features is correspondingly limited, and tree-based ensembles capture the nonlinear interactions between these short-window features more efficiently than deep models can without additional sequencing signal to exploit.

The near-identical performance at NTL (0.780) and ATL (0.770) reflects the fact that loading-dominated slab formation operates in essentially the same regime across these two bands. The approximately 2 °C of cooling between NTL and ATL is small relative to the temperature thresholds that govern whether falling precipitation produces a cohesive slab—primarily, whether new snow accumulates as dry powder, falls through partial melting, or arrives as rain. On most loading days in continental Colorado, both bands lie comfortably on the dry-snow side of that threshold, and the daily snowfall they receive after orographic adjustment differs by only a fraction of an inch. The result is that storm-driven slab formation is governed by the same short-window loading patterns at both bands, and the models converge to similar macro-F1.

The drop in performance at BTL (0.672) is interpretable through the same physical lens. BTL temperatures average approximately 4 °C warmer than ATL, and several consequences follow. First, dry-snow slab formation is interrupted more frequently by precipitation falling near or above freezing, by partial melting of newly deposited snow, and by warm-air-driven destabilization of recent storm layers—all of which reduce the prevalence of operationally identified Slab Problem at BTL. The dataset reflects this directly: Slab Problem is present on 9.56% of BTL records, compared with 32.62% at NTL and 41.27% at ATL. With fewer positive examples and noisier feature–label relationships, the same short-window loading features carry weaker signal at BTL, and the model’s macro-F1 reflects the combined effect of reduced prevalence and a less coherent physical regime. The absence of wind observations limits how confidently any of these models can distinguish wind-slab from storm-slab formation; we return to this point in §4.1.

#### 3.1.2 Persistent slab

A 64-unit, two-layer Transformer is the best-performing architecture for Persistent Slab at all three elevation bands, achieving macro-F1 of 0.746 at BTL, 0.656 at NTL, and 0.762 at ATL. Persistent Slab forms when a buried weak layer, typically composed of faceted crystals or surface hoar, develops over multiple weeks beneath an accumulating overlying slab. Its formation requires sustained cold periods that promote temperature-gradient faceting, and its persistence requires that subsequent loading and temperature conditions not disrupt the weak layer before a cohesive overlying slab forms (Conlan and Jamieson, 2016). Because this evolution unfolds over weeks rather than days, models that can integrate long-range temporal context have an inherent advantage. The Transformer’s attention mechanism allows the model to weight individual days within an extended lookback window according to their relevance to weak-layer development, capturing the storm cycles, faceting intervals, and warming events that determine whether a persistent slab matures or dissipates.

The strongest performance occurs at ATL (0.762), and the physical interpretation is straightforward. ATL temperatures are the coldest of the three bands, sustained cold periods are longest, and melt–freeze cycling is least frequent. Surface hoar and near-surface faceted layers form and remain undisturbed for the multi-week intervals required to evolve into operationally relevant weak layers, and the cumulative snowfall and snowpack signal that drives an overlying slab is correspondingly clean. The Transformer’s best ATL configuration uses a relatively short 7-day attention window, indicating that the recent meteorological context—combined with the long-window aggregate features already in the feature set—is sufficient to characterize ATL conditions without longer explicit memory.

At BTL, performance is slightly lower (0.746) but the best Transformer configuration uses a 14-day attention window—twice the lookback of the ATL model. This difference is physically interpretable. BTL conditions are dominated by more transient warming events, more frequent rain-on-snow occurrences, and more variable bonding within the upper snowpack, all of which can disrupt weak-layer development over the multi-week intervals during which a persistent slab is forming. To recover the underlying persistent-slab signal under these noisier conditions, the model needs a longer attention window that allows it to filter individual warming or melt events and identify the sustained cold periods when weak-layer development actually proceeds. The fact that the attention window itself shifts with elevation in a way that tracks the physical complexity of the local snowpack environment supports the interpretation that the model is exploiting genuine temporal structure rather than memorizing band-specific feature distributions.

NTL exhibits the lowest macro-F1 of the three bands (0.656), a pattern that initially appears surprising given that Persistent Slab is highly prevalent at NTL (74.98%) and the band sits between two regimes that the model handles well. The physical interpretation is precisely that NTL inherits the worst of both. Temperatures at NTL average approximately 2 °C warmer than ATL, which is enough to introduce more frequent intermittent warming, more frequent melt–freeze cycling, and more variable bonding during the long intervals over which weak layers develop, but not enough to fundamentally shift NTL out of the dry-snow weak-layer-forming regime. The result is a band on which persistent slabs form frequently but on which the multi-week temporal sequences that lead to weak-layer formation are systematically noisier than at ATL. The Transformer’s best NTL configuration uses a reduced learning rate (5 × 10 −4 rather than the 1 × 10 −3 default), consistent with optimization on a harder signal-to-noise regime. The combination of high prevalence and noisier physics explains why this band is the hardest for any architecture on this target.

#### 3.1.3 Loose Wet

Performance on the Loose Wet target is the strongest of the three problem types in aggregate (mean macro-F1 = 0.754 across bands), reflecting the fact that its physical drivers, positive temperatures, melt–freeze cycling, and rain-on-snow events, are captured directly and unambiguously in the meteorological feature set. Loose-wet instability is also conceptually simpler than slab-based problems: it does not depend on the integrity of a buried weak layer or on the cohesion properties of an overlying slab, but on whether liquid water is being introduced into the snowpack at rates that destabilize surface cohesion. Where the temperature features cross meaningful melt thresholds, the signal is largely self-evident.

The architectural split between bands maps onto a difference in the temporal character of Loose Wet activity. At BTL, a 128-unit, two-layer GRU with a 7-day lookback achieves the best macro-F1 (0.750). BTL receives intermittent melt episodes throughout the season—including mid-winter warm spells, early-spring isothermal episodes, and rain-on-snow events that occur sporadically rather than in a single seasonal cluster—and the precise timing of warming relative to surrounding snow conditions carries information about whether a given warm interval will produce operationally relevant loose-wet activity. The GRU’s recurrent processing of the daily temperature and snowfall sequence captures this timing structure in a way that the rolling aggregates alone do not.

At NTL and ATL, tree-based ensembles win: ExtraTrees with 200 estimators at NTL (0.747) and ExtraTrees with 300 estimators at ATL (0.764). Loose Wet at these higher bands is governed primarily by sustained spring warming, when the snowpack transitions toward isothermal conditions, and meltwater begins percolating through the column. This is a more punctuated, more seasonally concentrated phenomenon than the year-round melt activity at BTL, and it is well-characterized by the rolling 7-day, 30-day, and 60-day temperature aggregates already in the feature set. With the temporal pattern effectively encoded by the rolling features, the additional capacity of a sequence model offers no advantage, and the tree-based ensembles perform at parity or better. The lower prevalence of Loose Wet at ATL (7.59%, compared with 13.41% at NTL and 13.60% at BTL) is consistent with this picture: above-treeline conditions reach sustained melt thresholds for shorter portions of the season, and Loose Wet events at ATL cluster narrowly within late spring rather than recurring through the winter.

Recurrent and attention-based architectures achieve the highest macro-F1 across all three elevation bands at Stage 2, and the specific architectural choice tracks the physical complexity of the hazard signal at each band. Overall danger is an inherently temporal multi-process target: it integrates short-term loading from storm and wind slabs, multi-week weak-layer evolution responsible for persistent slab, and melt-driven loose-wet activity, and it does so through an operational rating that reflects likelihood, size, and the interaction of whatever problem types are active on a given day. The Stage-1 problem-prediction features arrive at Stage 2 as a heterogeneous mix of short- and long-window signals, and the deep sequence-aware architectures are better positioned than tree-based ensembles to align these signals temporally with the evolving hazard pattern.

At BTL, the best-performing architecture is a 128-unit, three-layer Transformer with 0.3 dropout, the deepest Stage-2 model fit at any band. The depth and width of this architecture are interpretable through the physical character of BTL danger. BTL is the band on which all three problem types are simultaneously active most often within the same season: dry-snow slab problems during cold loading events, persistent slab during sustained cold intervals (when those occur at this warmer band), and loose-wet activity throughout much of the season. The hazard signal at BTL is therefore an unusually heterogeneous mixture, and the attention mechanism’s ability to weight different feature signals differently at different points in the temporal context allows the model to integrate these problem-type signals more effectively than a recurrent model that processes them through a single hidden state.

At NTL and ATL, the best-performing architecture is the same in both bands: a 128-unit, two-layer SimpleRNN with 0.3 dropout, trained with a reduced learning rate of 5 × 10 −4. The convergence to the same architecture at these two bands reflects a convergence in physical regime. Both bands are dominated by slab and persistent-slab activity, with Loose Wet present but less central. The hazard signal is more uniform in physical character at NTL and ATL than at BTL, and the recurrent processing of the temporal sequence—without attention weighting across positions—is sufficient to integrate the signal. The reduced learning rate at both bands is consistent with the noisier optimization regime that arises from the more difficult class boundary between Moderate (Class 1) and Considerable (Class 2), which is where most of the per-day classification difficulty lies at these elevations.

The headline macro-F1 ranking, BTL (0.544) > NTL (0.525) > ATL (0.508), runs counter to the pattern observed at Stage 1, where Slab Problem and Persistent Slab both performed better at higher elevations. The reversal is interpretable through the structure of the multiclass danger label. At BTL, the dataset skews heavily toward Class 0 (Low, 49.64% of band records), and the most physically distinct boundary in the data, separating Low-danger days from any elevated-hazard day, is comparatively easy to identify from temperature and snowpack features alone. At NTL and ATL, the dominant class shifts to Class 1 (Moderate, 55.63% and 56.75% of records, respectively), and the operationally consequential boundaries—Moderate vs. Considerable, and Considerable vs. High—depend on subtler combinations of problem-type activity, snowpack structure, and spatial variability that the feature set encodes only partially. The lower macro-F1 at higher elevations is therefore not evidence that the model captures less physical signal at those bands; it reflects that the operational task at those bands is intrinsically harder.

The model’s per-class performance varies systematically across elevation bands in a way that previews the operational findings in §3.3. Across all three bands, the model performs most strongly on Class 0 (Low danger, F1 = 0.580–0.805) and Class 1 (Moderate, F1 = 0.515–0.578), as expected given these are the dominant classes in the dataset. Performance on Class 2 (Considerable) is more variable (F1 = 0.436–0.483), reflecting the difficulty of the boundary between Moderate and Considerable, which is where the operational task is intrinsically hardest. The most consequential per-class result, however, is Class 3 (High danger): F1 = 0.341 at BTL, 0.457 at NTL, and 0.504 at ATL—a monotonic increase with elevation despite High danger being the rarest class at every band. We return to this Class 3 performance pattern in §3.3.3, where the comparison against a prior-art Random Forest baseline isolates its operational significance.

The dominant feature of the full-period results is the strength of 1-day persistence. Across all nine Stage-1 cells, Pers1d ranges from macro-F1 = 0.728 to 0.969, exceeding the corresponding model macro-F1 in most cells. The same pattern is even more pronounced at Stage 2, where Pers1d reaches 0.644–0.698 across the three bands, substantially above the model’s 0.508–0.544 on this full-period evaluation. Climatology performs near the trivial floor, as expected.

The strength of 1-day persistence on full-period evaluation is not an indictment of the model: it is a property of the joint forecaster–snowpack system. CAIC forecasters issue each day’s rating with explicit awareness of the previous day’s rating, and the underlying snowpack evolves over timescales of hours to weeks rather than between adjacent days. Persistence at lag 1 therefore captures both the autocorrelation introduced by forecaster behavior and the autocorrelation inherent in the physical system: weak layers that existed yesterday almost always exist today, storm cycles that were loading yesterday are usually still resolving today, and a snowpack that was isothermal yesterday morning is unlikely to have refrozen by today morning. As lag increases (Pers3d → Pers7d → Pers14d), persistence performance degrades monotonically in nearly every cell, confirming that the autocorrelation benefit decays over the same timescales as the underlying physical processes. The implication is not that the model adds no value, but rather that full-period macro-F1 — which is dominated by the many days on which the rating is unchanged from yesterday—measures the wrong thing if the goal is to characterize model contribution beyond autocorrelation. The transitions-only analysis in §3.3.2 isolates the days on which the issued rating changes and provides the operationally meaningful comparison.

#### 3.3.2 Transitions-only analysis

We define a transitions day at a given (band, target) cell as any day in the Stage-2 evaluation window on which the issued label differs from the label issued on the previous day. Inherently, 1-day persistence achieves macro-F1 = 0 on this subset: it always predicts the prior day’s class, which is by definition wrong on a transition day. Climatology retains a non-trivial macro-F1 on transitions days because the most-frequent class is sometimes the correct post-transition class. The transitions subset therefore isolates the question of whether the model contributes useful signal beyond what autocorrelation alone provides.

The Stage-2 transitions result is the central operational finding of this section. On the subset of days when the issued danger rating changes from the previous day—that is, when a forecaster is actively reassessing conditions in response to evolving snowpack or weather—the proposed model achieves macro-F1 substantially above climatology (BTL 0.294 vs. 0.113; NTL 0.437 vs. 0.151; ATL 0.402 vs. 0.151) and substantially above 1-day persistence (0.000 at all three bands), with paired permutation p < 0.001 against both baselines at every band. The physical interpretation is direct: transitions occur on days when the snowpack or weather has crossed a threshold that warrants an updated assessment—the start or end of a storm cycle, the first sustained warming of spring, the onset of a cold spell that initiates weak-layer development, the arrival of rain at elevations where snow had previously been falling. Each of these transitions has distinct meteorological signatures encoded in the model’s feature set, and the model is able to recover these signatures from the daily and rolling-window features even when the previous day’s rating provides no guidance. The model is operating on the physics directly, rather than on the forecaster’s prior, and the magnitude of the gap against persistence on these days is the strongest available evidence that the framework has learned operationally relevant structure.

At Stage 1, the model significantly outperforms climatology in six of the nine (band, target) cells. The 3 cells that do not reach significance—NTL Persistent Slab (n = 32), ATL Persistent Slab (n = 17), and ATL Loose Wet (n = 39) — share the property that transitions are rare at higher elevations for these problem types. Once a persistent slab is established at NTL or ATL, the multi-week intervals required to dissipate the underlying weak layer mean the problem typically remains present for extended periods, and the corresponding transitions are infrequent; similarly, once Loose Wet activity ends at ATL with the close of the spring melt window, it does not typically recur within the same season. The small sample sizes that result reflect physical reality rather than model deficiency: there are simply not many days at these (band, target) cells on which the issued problem indicator changes, and the statistical power to detect even moderate effects against climatology is correspondingly limited.

Among the baselines, the per-band logistic model is the strongest in mean macro-F1 (0.457), exceeding both tree ensembles and the best-tuned Random Forest, and it approaches the pipeline at NTL (0.496 vs. 0.525) and ATL (0.489 vs. 0.508) while remaining well behind at BTL (0.385 vs. 0.544).

Three architectural components of the proposed framework account for this margin, each interpretable through the physics of the underlying processes. First, the framework trains separate models per elevation band, while the Pérez-Guillén Random Forest pools the three bands into a single model with elevation-band one-hot indicators. The physical regimes differ substantially—BTL is dominated by heterogeneous melt and loading activity, ATL by sustained dry-snow weak-layer evolution, and NTL by a transitional mixture—and a single pooled model must compromise across them. Per-band models can specialize, and the gap is largest at BTL (+0.146), the band whose physics differs most sharply from the others. Part of the pipeline’s margin over the prior-art Random Forest is therefore attributable to this pooling penalty, and the logistic results make the point directly: fit separately per band, the logistic model already incorporates this same per-band specialization, which is why we treat it as a quasi-baseline rather than an independent control, and why its gap to the pipeline collapses from +0.158 at BTL to +0.029 at NTL and +0.019 at ATL. A per-band linear model recovers most of the available signal at the two bands whose danger structure is more linearly accessible, but fails at heterogeneous BTL, where temporal and structural capacity matter most. Reported as a partial framework, the logistic results reinforce the architectural argument rather than undercutting it.

Second, the framework predicts avalanche problem types as an explicit intermediate stage, and the Stage-2 model conditions its danger estimate on the inferred failure mechanisms rather than on raw meteorology alone. Including the three Stage-1 problem predictions as Stage-2 features gives the model direct access to this intermediate structure, which a single-stage baseline must instead recover implicitly. Third, the framework uses recurrent and attention-based architectures that explicitly model temporal evolution, while the baselines operate on individual feature vectors without notion of sequence; as established in §3.1 and §3.2, deep sequence-aware models recover signal from the multi-day evolution of meteorological and snowpack states that a feature-vector model cannot.

The starkest contrast among the baselines appears on High-danger (Class 3) prediction, evaluated here in a common single-model regime so that all models are compared on the same footing. The tree ensembles effectively fail to identify Class 3 days: XGBoost reaches Class 3 F1 of 0.000, 0.128, and 0.128 across BTL, NTL, and ATL; LightGBM 0.000, 0.047, and 0.048; and the best-tuned pooled Random Forest 0.094. The Random Forest confusion matrix (Table 11) makes the failure mode concrete: across the 4,221-row held-out period it predicts Class 3 only five times against 101 true Class 3 days (precision 1.000, recall 0.050). The per-band logistic model recovers more of the rare-class signal (0.118, 0.382, 0.365), and the pipeline leads it clearly at the two lower bands (0.323 vs. 0.118 at BTL; 0.463 vs. 0.382 at NTL) while reaching a near-tie at ATL (0.388 vs. 0.365). The pipeline therefore dramatically outperforms the tree ensembles on Class 3 — which collapse to near-zero—and leads or matches the linear quasi-baseline, with its clearest margins at the bands where rare-class signal is otherwise hardest to recover.
