### 3.4 Summary of key findings

Three cross-cutting patterns emerge from the results above.

First, model-family selection is governed by the temporal scale of the prediction target. Tree-based ensembles are most effective for Slab Problem at all three elevation bands, where the collinearity of 1-, 3-, and 7-day rolling aggregates already encodes sequencing information in tabular form, reducing the marginal benefit of explicit sequence modeling. Attention-based Transformer architectures are uniformly most effective for Persistent Slab, where multi-week weak-layer evolution and the integration of long-window snowfall and snowpack signals require explicit temporal modeling. Loose Wet is mixed: a sequence model wins at BTL, where melt timing is highly variable and Loose Wet is comparatively prevalent, while tree-based ensembles win at NTL and ATL, where melt events occur in more punctuated clusters that rolling aggregates capture sufficiently. Overall danger at Stage 2 is dominated by recurrent and attention-based architectures across all three bands, consistent with its character as a multi-process temporal target.

Second, elevation systematically shapes both class distribution and problem prevalence. Slab Problem prevalence increases monotonically with elevation (BTL 9.56%, NTL 32.62%, ATL 41.27%), and Slab Problem performance increases with elevation in the same direction. Persistent Slab prevalence also increases sharply with elevation (BTL 26.68%, NTL 74.98%, ATL 77.92%), driven by the more sustained cold periods needed for weak-layer development at higher bands. Loose Wet prevalence runs counter to both, decreasing with elevation as warmer below- and near-treeline conditions more frequently support melt-driven instability. Stage-2 overall-danger class distribution shifts from Low-dominated at BTL toward Moderate-dominated at NTL and ATL, with consequential Class 2 (Considerable) and Class 3 (High) days remaining rare at every band.

Third, the proposed pipeline captures signal on the days that matter most operationally. On full-period evaluation, 1-day persistence is a deceptively strong baseline because operational ratings are inherently autocorrelated, and physical snowpack states evolve slowly. On the subset of days when the rating changes from the previous day, the days a forecaster is actively reassessing, the proposed model significantly outperforms both persistence and climatology at every Stage-2 elevation band (p < 0.001 in every case). On the same eight-zone Colorado dataset, the proposed two-stage per-band pipeline outperforms a Pérez-Guillén-style Random Forest reproduction by +0.131 macro-F1 averaged across bands, with non-overlapping bootstrap 95% confidence intervals at all three bands. The largest operational contrast lies in High-danger (Class 3) prediction. The prior-art Pérez-Guillén-exact configuration reaches Class 3 F1 = 0.020, and a best-tuned Random Forest only 0.094, predicting Class 3 just five times in 4,221 days against 101 true positives, while the proposed pipeline achieves Class 3 F1 of 0.341, 0.457, and 0.504 across the three elevation bands, a 3.6× to 5.4× improvement over the best-tuned baseline, with Class 3 recall as high as 0.725 at ATL.

## 4 Discussion

The results in §3 establish three distinct findings about the proposed two-stage framework: that its architectural choices recover known avalanche-formation physics, that it outperforms prior-art single-stage approaches on the same dataset, and that it captures forecast-relevant signal on the transition days when persistence-based baselines fail by construction. This Discussion develops these findings and addresses the questions they raise. §4.1 interprets the relationship between model architecture and the temporal scale of each prediction target through the lens of avalanche formation physics. §4.2 articulates the three-legged contribution of this work as a single integrated argument. §4.3 examines the dependence between the Stage-1 problem labels and the Stage-2 danger target, establishing that the two-stage gain does not arise from the shared forecasting origin of the two label sets. §4.4 examines the operational implications for High-danger (Class 3) prediction, where the contrast against prior-art baselines is most consequential for deployment. §4.5 situates the framework within the broader context of data-sparse avalanche forecasting and discusses considerations for generalization beyond Colorado. §4.6 enumerates the limitations of the present study and identifies directions for future work.

### 4.1 Alignment with avalanche formation physics

A central interpretive finding of this work is the alignment between model behavior and established avalanche formation physics. The architectural pattern that emerges from the nine Stage-1 (band, problem) cells maps onto the temporal scale of the underlying physical processes with little ambiguity. Tree-based ensembles dominate Slab Problem at all three elevation bands, where the dominant drivers—storm-driven loading, recent temperature evolution, and short-term bonding within the upper snowpack—operate over hours to a few days. The collinear 1-, 3-, and 7-day rolling features that capture these processes already encode much of the relevant temporal structure in tabular form, and the nonlinear interactions among them are well-captured by tree-based learners. Attention-based Transformer architectures dominate Persistent Slab at all three bands, where buried weak-layer formation unfolds over weeks of sustained cold conditions punctuated by loading and warming events; the attention mechanism’s ability to weight individual days within an extended lookback window is well-matched to this multi-week evolution. Loose Wet, governed by positive temperatures and melt–freeze cycling, shows a split pattern: a recurrent architecture wins at BTL, where melt events are frequent and irregular through the season, while tree-based ensembles win at NTL and ATL, where Loose Wet activity occurs in punctuated late-season clusters that the rolling temperature and snowpack aggregates already characterize sufficiently.

Two finer-grained patterns reinforce this interpretation. First, the optimal Transformer lookback window for Persistent Slab shifts with elevation in a physically interpretable direction: 7 days at ATL, where weak-layer development proceeds under cold and stable conditions; 14 days at BTL, where warmer temperatures, more frequent rain-on-snow events, and more variable bonding require the model to filter individual disruptions and identify the sustained cold intervals when weak-layer development actually occurs. Second, the optimization regime shifts with the noisiness of the underlying signal: the NTL Persistent Slab Transformer requires a reduced learning rate (5 × 10 −4) compared to the default at ATL and BTL, consistent with NTL inheriting the worst of both worlds: high prevalence but systematically noisier weak-layer-evolution sequences. These patterns emerged from data-driven hyperparameter selection rather than physical priors imposed by the framework, and their consistency with physical expectation supports the interpretation that the models have learned operationally meaningful structure rather than memorizing band-specific feature distributions.

The Stage-2 architectural choices align with the same physical reasoning. Recurrent and attention-based models dominate overall danger prediction at every band, consistent with overall danger being an inherently temporal multi-process target that integrates short-term loading, multi-week weak-layer evolution, and melt-driven instability simultaneously. The deeper Transformer at BTL responds to the unusually heterogeneous mix of problem types active there within the same season; the convergent two-layer SimpleRNN solution at NTL and ATL reflects the more uniform slab-and-persistent-slab dominance of those bands.

### 4.2 Three legged contribution

The contribution of this work rests on three findings, each established empirically in §3 and physically interpretable in terms of avalanche formation processes.

First, two-stage classification is necessary for recovering the rare High-danger (Class 3) days. Predicting avalanche problem types as an explicit intermediate stage and passing those predictions forward as structured features into the danger-rating stage produces the largest gains precisely on the high-consequence days a single-stage model fails to surface (§3.3.3, §4.3). The mechanism is straightforward: operational danger ratings are not a direct function of weather inputs but reflect a forecaster’s assessment of which avalanche processes are currently active and how those processes combine. A two-stage architecture provides explicit representational capacity for this intermediate structure, while a single-stage model is forced to recover problem-type information implicitly from the same meteorological features that determine the eventual danger estimate.

Second, per-band sequence models outperform pooled tree-based approaches on the same dataset. On the eight-zone Colorado dataset used in this study, the proposed two-stage per-band pipeline outperforms a Pérez-Guillén-style Random Forest reproduction by +0.146 macro-F1 at BTL, +0.131 at NTL, and +0.114 at ATL, a mean improvement of +0.131, with non-overlapping bootstrap 95% confidence intervals at all three bands. A best-tuned Random Forest swept across five additional configurations closes only +0.024 of this gap, confirming the difference is not an artifact of hyperparameter choice. Three architectural features drive the gain: per-band specialization, which lets each model adapt to the distinct physical regime of its elevation band; the two-stage operational structure described above; and the explicit temporal modeling that recurrent and attention-based architectures provide.

Third, the model captures signal on transition days where persistence collapses. On full-period evaluation, 1-day persistence is a deceptively strong baseline: operational ratings are inherently autocorrelated, and the underlying snowpack evolves slowly. A naive forecaster who simply reissued yesterday’s rating every day would appear to outperform the model on aggregate macro-F1. The transitions-only evaluation in §3.3.2 isolates the subset of days when the issued rating changes from the previous day, removing the autocorrelation contribution and asking whether the model captures genuine signal on the days when forecasters are actively reassessing. On this evaluation, the proposed model significantly outperforms both climatology and 1-day persistence at every Stage-2 elevation band (paired permutation p < 0.001 in all cases). The physical interpretation is direct: transition days correspond to moments when the snowpack or weather has crossed a threshold warranting an updated assessment—the start or end of a storm cycle, the onset of sustained warming or cooling, the arrival of rain at an elevation where snow had previously been falling—and each of these transitions has distinct meteorological signatures encoded in the model’s feature set. The model recovers these signatures from the daily and rolling-window features even when the previous day’s rating provides no guidance, which is the strongest available evidence that the framework has learned operationally relevant structure rather than exploited autocorrelation in the target.

These three contributions are not independent. The operational two-stage structure provides the representational capacity that allows the per-band sequence models to exploit problem-type co-occurrence, which is in turn what allows the framework to recover signal on transition days where multiple processes are simultaneously evolving.

### 4.3 Stage dependence between problem and danger targets

Because operational avalanche problems and danger ratings are issued together by the same forecaster, a reasonable concern is whether the two-stage gain arises from this shared origin rather than from added predictive structure. Inherently, it cannot: the Stage-2 danger model never receives the forecaster-issued problem labels. It consumes only the predicted problem types from the frozen Stage-1 ensembles (§2.5.5), which are functions of the meteorological and snowpack inputs alone and are generated out-of-sample with respect to Stage-1 training. Conditioning the danger stage on these inferred problems reproduces the structure of operational forecasting, in which problems are assessed first and the integrated danger rating is formed from them, rather than reusing any label co-issued with the danger rating the model is trained to predict.

### 4.4 Operational implications for high-danger prediction

The most operationally consequential finding of this work concerns the model’s performance on High-danger (Class 3) days. Class 3 is the threshold at which forecaster guidance most strongly drives backcountry travel decisions: very dangerous avalanche conditions exist, and human-triggered avalanches are very likely, and it is also the rarest class in the dataset at every elevation band. The Pérez-Guillén-style Random Forest reproduction predicts Class 3 only five times across the entire 4,221-row held-out period, against 101 true Class 3 days, yielding a per-class F1 of 0.094 and the Pérez-Guillén-exact configuration is worse still at 0.020. The proposed two-stage pipeline achieves Class 3 F1 of 0.341 at BTL, 0.457 at NTL, and 0.504 at ATL, improvements of 3.6×, 4.9×, and 5.4× respectively over the best-tuned Random Forest, with Class 3 recall climbing as high as 0.725 at ATL.

The physical interpretation of the Random Forest’s failure mode is that Class 3 days are characterized not by any single meteorological feature crossing a threshold but by the simultaneous activity of multiple problem types: a fresh dry-snow slab loading event on top of a pre-existing persistent weak layer, or a rapid warming event onto an already-loaded snowpack. These combinations are rare in the training data and lie in regions of feature space sparsely populated by individual class examples. A pooled single-stage model trained to produce a single class label from a single feature vector has no mechanism for explicitly representing problem-type co-occurrence; during inference it systematically defaults to lower-danger predictions on the rarest and most consequential conditions. The proposed two-stage pipeline, by contrast, flags multiple problem types simultaneously at Stage 1 and passes that co-occurrence signal explicitly into Stage 2. This is what allows it to surface Class 3 days the Random Forest entirely misses.

One pattern in the Class 3 results merits particular attention. The aggregate Stage-2 macro-F1 ranking (BTL 0.544, NTL 0.525, ATL 0.508) suggests that performance is highest at the lowest elevation band, which would be a counterintuitive operational conclusion given that the most consequential avalanche terrain in Colorado is concentrated near and above treeline. At the per-class level, however, this ranking reverses on the most consequential class: Class 3 F1 increases monotonically with elevation (BTL 0.341, NTL 0.457, ATL 0.504), driven by both higher Class 3 prevalence and cleaner co-occurrence signals at the higher bands. The macro-F1 ranking is dominated by the easy Class 0 (Low) boundary at BTL, where 49.64% of records are Low-danger and the boundary between Low and any elevated-hazard class is comparatively easy to identify. The operational ranking, performance on the days when forecaster guidance most strongly determines backcountry decisions, runs in the opposite direction. For deployment purposes, the operational ranking is the relevant one, and it points toward the elevation bands where consequential avalanche terrain is concentrated.

### 4.5 Generalization and deployment context

A central finding of this work is that models trained exclusively on accessible meteorological features—snowfall, temperature, and simple derived snowpack aggregates—can produce operationally meaningful predictions in a continental snow climate without specialized atmospheric inputs. Pérez-Guillén et al. (2022) reached macro-F1 = 0.70 in the Swiss Alps using more than fifty times the data volume of this study and incorporating wind speed, humidity, radiation, and detailed snowpack-layer variables; that performance ceiling is not directly comparable to the present results because of fundamental differences in snow climate, evaluation protocol, and data construction pipeline, but the comparison establishes that feature-rich approaches set a real upper bound on what is achievable on this task. The contribution of the present work is to demonstrate that operationally useful signal exists below that ceiling on a substantially reduced input space, and that careful architectural choices—two-stage operational structure, per-band specialization, temporal modeling—can recover much of that signal. This is the result that matters for regions lacking the instrumentation infrastructure or operational forecasting services that feature-rich approaches require, and it is consistent with the broader objective of expanding avalanche forecasting accessibility into data-sparse and resource-limited mountain environments.

The eight forecast regions included in this study were selected to span the major continental snow-climate sub-ranges of Colorado, including both well-instrumented zones with strong operational forecast coverage and zones with sparser ground-based observation networks. While all eight regions are within Colorado and therefore share a single broad climate classification, the diversity of station environments, storm-track positioning, and within-state subclimate variability provides a meaningful test of how the framework generalizes within a continental regime. The strongest deployment value of the framework lies at NTL and ATL, where both Class 3 performance and the underlying problem-type signals are most reliable, and where the majority of consequential backcountry avalanche terrain in Colorado is concentrated. The lower-elevation BTL band remains useful for capturing season-onset and warm-period transitions where loose-wet and short-term loading signals contribute to operational decision-making, but its lower Class 3 reliability suggests it should be interpreted in conjunction with, rather than as a substitute for, higher-band predictions when both are available.

### 4.6 Limitations

Despite the contributions described above, several limitations of the present study warrant explicit discussion.

First, Stage-2 macro-F1 is systematically lower on the second window (92.5%–100% of the chronological dataset) than on the immediately preceding out of sample window (85%–92.5%), by approximately 8 percentage points at BTL (first 0.583, second 0.505) and 10 percentage points at NTL (first 0.573, second 0.477) and ATL (first 0.557, second 0.458). This pattern, which is consistent across bands and across model architectures, is most plausibly attributed to a distribution shift in the post-2020 portion of the study period, possibly reflecting changes in CAIC operational forecasting practice, an unusual sequence of recent winter seasons, or a combination of both. We have not attempted to characterize this shift quantitatively in the present work, but its presence implies that the headline performance values reported here may overstate generalization to future seasons; reported performance should be interpreted as bounded above by the validation window and below by the test window, with the truth likely closer to the test value for forward-looking deployment scenarios.

Second, each of the eight CAIC forecast regions is paired with a single GHCN-Daily station in this study, selected to be representative of regional meteorological conditions on the windward side of the relevant mountain range. While this design choice was necessary to maintain consistent feature availability across all eight regions and the full study period, it does not capture within-region spatial heterogeneity in storm track exposure, aspect-dependent precipitation distribution, or microclimatic effects. CAIC forecast regions span tens to hundreds of square kilometers, and single-station meteorological inputs cannot fully represent this variability. Future work could explore multi-station aggregation within each forecast region, or the incorporation of gridded reanalysis products for additional spatial coverage.

Third, Class 4 conditions did not occur at any forecast region, day, or elevation band over the eight-region study period and were therefore not modeled as a separate class. The four-class scheme used here (Low, Moderate, Considerable, High) covers all conditions observed in the dataset but cannot be evaluated on Extreme conditions until additional Class 4 examples are available. The CAIC forecast archive in Colorado includes Class 4 conditions historically, but at frequencies that did not produce qualifying region-band-day records within the present study period. Future work could extend the temporal coverage to include earlier or later winter seasons that contain Class 4 events or incorporate forecast data from other continental-snow-climate regions where Class 4 conditions are more frequent.

Fourth, the Pérez-Guillén-style Random Forest reproduction used in §3.3.3 is implemented on the eight-zone Colorado dataset using the meteorological feature set available here, not on the full Swiss feature set used in the original publication. The comparison demonstrates that the proposed framework outperforms a published prior-art configuration applied to the same data, which is the relevant operational question for deployment in Colorado, but it does not directly benchmark the proposed framework against the original Pérez-Guillén results on Swiss data. A direct comparison would require either training the proposed framework on Swiss data with the full Swiss feature set or training the original Pérez-Guillén configuration on the Colorado dataset using Swiss-specific features that were not available here. Future work could pursue the first of these comparisons in collaboration with the Swiss avalanche research community.

Fifth, the meteorological feature set used here omits several variables known to influence avalanche formation, including wind speed and direction, relative humidity, solar radiation, and detailed snow stratigraphy. Their absence partially explains why the framework’s performance is bounded above by feature-rich approaches. This limitation is particularly important for the merged Slab Problem target, which combines storm slab and wind slab despite the absence of wind speed and wind direction predictors. The design choice to merge these problem types was made to preserve a practically relevant slab-instability target under sparse-data conditions, but it reduces mechanistic specificity. In particular, the model is not expected to distinguish whether predicted slab conditions arise primarily from snowfall loading or wind redistribution. Future work should separate storm slab and wind slab once wind observations or reanalysis-derived wind transport proxies are available.

Sixth, avalanche danger ratings issued by CAIC contain inherent expert judgment, particularly below treeline, where local terrain, tree cover, and microclimatic effects complicate forecasting. While the CAIC is widely recognized as one of the premier avalanche forecasting centers in North America, this subjectivity introduces noise into the labels used for both training and evaluation. The model can match the issued ratings only insofar as those ratings themselves are consistent across forecasters and across days; any forecaster-to-forecaster variation in how the same physical conditions are categorized propagates into the training targets and the evaluation metric.

Seventh, the dataset exhibits the class imbalance characteristic of operational avalanche forecasting records, with Class 3 (High) occurring on only 2.27% of all region-band-days. While the proposed framework substantially outperforms baseline approaches on Class 3 prediction, the absolute number of Class 3 days available for evaluation is small (101 across both windows pooled), and individual Class 3 F1 values should be interpreted with appropriate uncertainty.

Eighth, the altitude-adjusted snowfall and temperature features rely on fixed empirical values: a 7% per-1000-ft orographic snowfall multiplier and a 6.1 °C km -1 temperature lapse rate. These values are standard in operational snow modeling but introduce approximation error, particularly in shoulder seasons and during atmospheric conditions where lapse rates depart substantially from the dry adiabatic value. Future work could incorporate variable lapse rates derived from radiosonde or reanalysis data, or propagate uncertainty in the scaling relationships through to the downstream danger predictions.

Ninth, although the framework’s discrimination performance is promising, its predicted-probability calibration degrades with elevation: expected calibration error rises from BTL to ATL, and the model grows increasingly overconfident at the higher bands, where mean predicted confidence exceeds empirical accuracy by a widening margin. For a high-stakes forecasting application, miscalibration of this kind is operationally consequential—an overconfident High-danger probability is interpreted differently from a well-calibrated one—and it is most pronounced precisely at the upper bands where consequential avalanche terrain is concentrated. Post-hoc recalibration, such as temperature scaling fit on a held-out window, is the natural deployment-time remedy and does not require retraining; we flag it as a priority for future work rather than addressing it here.

Finally, this study evaluates the framework exclusively within Colorado’s continental snow climate. Although the eight regions span diverse within-state subclimates, storm tracks, and instrumentation densities, they share a single broad climate classification, and the results therefore characterize within-climate generalization only. They do not establish that the framework transfers to maritime (e.g., the Cascades, European maritime ranges) or intermountain (e.g., the Sierra Nevada, the Wasatch) regimes, which differ substantially in storm structure, snowpack evolution, and the relative frequency of avalanche problem types. We regard evaluation on an external region in a different snow climate as a necessary precondition for deployment claims beyond the continental regime; future work could pursue cross-climate training experiments in which the framework is trained on Colorado data and evaluated on out-of-climate test sets, ideally in collaboration with avalanche services holding such data.

## 5 Conclusion

This study introduces a two-stage classification framework for predicting avalanche problems and overall danger levels across elevation bands in Colorado, evaluated on a substantially expanded eight-region dataset spanning the major continental snow-climate sub-ranges of the state. The framework first predicts the presence of three distinct avalanche problem types, Slab Problem, Persistent Slab, and Loose Wet, at each elevation band, then uses these problem-type predictions as structured inputs to a second-stage danger-rating classifier. Architectures are trained separately per elevation band, with forecast region included as a one-hot feature to preserve site-level structure within a pooled training dataset, and models are evaluated using a staged chronological splitting protocol designed to prevent temporal leakage between stages.

Three findings emerge from the evaluation. First, the architectural patterns selected by the framework align consistently with the physical timescales of the underlying processes: tree-based ensembles dominate Slab Problem prediction, attention-based architectures dominate Persistent Slab, and recurrent and attention-based models dominate overall danger. Second, the framework outperforms a Pérez-Guillén-style Random Forest reproduction on the same eight-zone Colorado dataset by +0.131 macro-F1 averaged across bands, with non-overlapping bootstrap 95% confidence intervals at every elevation band. Third, on the subset of days when the issued danger rating changes from the previous day, the days when forecasters are actively reassessing conditions and persistence-based baselines collapse to macro-F1 = 0, the framework significantly outperforms both climatology and 1-day persistence at every elevation band.

The most operationally consequential result of this work concerns High-danger (Class 3) prediction. The proposed framework achieves Class 3 F1 of 0.341 at BTL, 0.457 at NTL, and 0.504 at ATL, representing 3.6× to 5.4× improvements over a best-tuned Random Forest baseline that achieves Class 3 F1 = 0.094 on the same data. The contrast between the prior-art baseline’s near-zero Class 3 recall and the proposed framework’s recall on the same days is the central operational finding of this study and motivates the architectural choices—explicit problem-type intermediate predictions, per-band specialization, and temporal modeling—that distinguish the framework from single-stage approaches. Together, these results establish a viable path forward for applying machine learning to avalanche forecasting in regions that lack the instrumentation infrastructure required by feature-rich approaches, and they provide evidence that meaningful hazard signal can be extracted from widely available meteorological observations when paired with operationally informed architectural design.

Our work introduces a viable path forward for applying machine learning to avalanche forecasting in data-limited environments, and it provides the first evidence that a two-stage architecture can enhance danger-level prediction in a continental snow climate. Continued development of this framework may contribute to more consistent, data-driven hazard assessments and support safer decision-making for both forecasters and backcountry travelers.
